The alternative annotator test

Source: R/core-stats-alttest.R
hr_alt_test.Rd

Tests whether a model's labels can be used in place of human annotators, with the leave-one-out procedure of Calderon, Reichart and Dror (2025) as implemented in their reference code (github.com/nitaytech/alttest).

Usage

hr_alt_test(
  model_labels,
  human_labels,
  expertise,
  epsilon = NULL,
  q = 0.05,
  metric = c("accuracy", "neg_rmse")
)

Arguments

model_labels

The model's label for each item: a vector with one value per row of human_labels, NA where it gave none.

human_labels

A matrix or data frame, items in rows and human annotators in columns, NA where an annotator did not label an item. Column names, when given, must be unique and non-empty; they name the rows of per_annotator.

expertise

The annotators' expertise: "expert", "skilled" or "crowd". Required.

epsilon

The cost-benefit margin. NULL takes it from expertise.

q

False discovery rate for the Benjamini-Yekutieli correction.

metric

"accuracy" for categorical labels, "neg_rmse" for numeric ones.

Value

An object of class hr_alt_test, a list with passed, omega, rho, epsilon, expertise, q, metric, n_items, per_annotator (a data frame: annotator, n, rho_model, rho_human, p_value, p_adjusted, rejected), sweep (a data frame of epsilon, omega and passed), skipped and notes.

Details

For each human annotator j in turn, on every item j labelled:

  1. score the model's label against the labels of the other annotators of that item, and score j's label the same way (metric: the share of them it matches for "accuracy", minus the root mean squared difference for "neg_rmse");

  2. W_model = 1 where the model's score is at least j's, W_human = 1 where j's is at least the model's (a tie counts for both);

  3. test H0: mean(W_human - W_model) >= epsilon against the one-sided alternative that it is below epsilon, with a one-sample t test. Rejecting says the model is not worse than j by more than epsilon.

The p-values of all annotators are corrected with Benjamini-Yekutieli at level q. The winning rate omega is the share of annotators for whom the test rejects, and the model passes when omega >= 0.5. The advantage probability rho is the mean of W_model over items, averaged over annotators: how often the model represents the others at least as well as the person it replaces.

epsilon is the penalty paid by the human annotators for being slower and dearer. The authors' rule of thumb sets it by their expertise: 0.2 for experts, 0.15 for skilled annotators such as trained students, 0.1 for crowd workers, and lower than that when the people agree poorly with each other. expertise has no default so the choice is always made on purpose. Because the verdict depends on epsilon, omega is also reported for each epsilon from 0.05 to 0.20 in steps of 0.05.

Requirements: at least 3 human annotators (the authors accept 2 but advise 3, since with two the test only asks which of them the model resembles), and at least 30 items with a model label and two or more human labels, where the t test's normal approximation starts to hold; fewer is an error. Below 50 items there is a warning, as the authors recommend 50 to 100. An annotator with fewer than 30 such items is left out of the test, as in the reference code, and the result names them.

A t statistic is undefined when W_human - W_model is constant. Then the p-value is 0 when that constant is below epsilon and 1 otherwise, the limit of the test as the spread goes to zero.

References

Calderon, N., Reichart, R. and Dror, R. (2025). The alternative annotator test for LLM-as-a-judge: how to statistically justify replacing human annotators with LLMs. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 16051-16081.

Benjamini, Y. and Yekutieli, D. (2001). The control of the false discovery rate in multiple testing under dependency. Annals of Statistics 29(4), 1165-1188.

See also

Other statistics: hr_agreement(), hr_ht_estimate(), hr_ppi(), hr_prop_ci()

Examples

set.seed(3)
gold <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 80, replace = TRUE)
noisy <- function(p) ifelse(runif(80) < p, gold, sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 80, TRUE))
people <- sapply(1:4, function(j) noisy(0.75))
hr_alt_test(noisy(0.95), people, expertise = "skilled")
#> <hr_alt_test> passed: omega = 1 with epsilon = 0.15 (skilled annotators), q = 0.05
#> 80 items, metric accuracy, advantage probability rho = 0.991
#> 
#>    annotator  n rho_model rho_human  p_value p_adjusted rejected
#>  annotator_1 80     0.988     0.850 1.15e-09   2.40e-09     TRUE
#>  annotator_2 80     0.988     0.800 2.17e-10   6.03e-10     TRUE
#>  annotator_3 80     0.988     0.788 1.34e-10   5.57e-10     TRUE
#>  annotator_4 80     1.000     0.825 2.58e-11   2.15e-10     TRUE
#> 
#> omega by epsilon:
#>  epsilon omega passed
#>     0.05     1   TRUE
#>     0.10     1   TRUE
#>     0.15     1   TRUE
#>     0.20     1   TRUE
